comments.author: @samyakshah806
comments.text:
True empires were only Mughal and Mauryan before the modern period. 

Delhi sultanate is the first instance of Delhi being used as a proper centre of power. It was never a true empire. It was mostly a feudal system with very different local systems. Mauryan and Mughal weren't surface level empires. They were centralized states. Mauryans did that from Patna. Mughals mostly did it from UP until later monarchs shifted to Delhi. 

The word "Sanskrit culture" is taking a lot of liberty. A better way to put it will be a continuous chain of urban centers that had overlapping cultural practices. It wasn't voluntary. The urban centers imposed upon local traditions and you will find all kinds of voluntary and involuntary means. 

Finally, the region wasn't as easy to navigate as it looks today. And the one frontier for defense argument doesn't hold because in times of stability the kingdom would have pushed further out but they never did. That frontier was often viewed as a buffer and a warning sign for the main capital to decide how to act. The truth is that the region was truly an empire only during the Mauryan and early Mughal period. Even that Mughal period of consolidation required significant absorption of regional power. Guptas don't even come close to a pan India empire. So there's a lot of over simplification here. But it's a good high level overview (even if inaccurate in places).

comments.author: @nipunverma123
comments.text:
If Europe can be recognised as a continent despite being physically connected to Asia, why can’t South Asia’s classification be challenged too?

Continental boundaries are not purely geological; history and convention shape how we divide the world. South Asia has a distinct geographical setting and a remarkably interconnected past. The Indus Valley civilisation, Gandhara, Ashoka’s inscriptions in present-day Afghanistan, and the Mauryan and Kushan empires reflect centuries of political, cultural and commercial connections across borders that exist today.

What if we recognised a proposed Indian Continent comprising eight countries?

- India
- Pakistan
- Bangladesh
- Afghanistan
- Nepal
- Bhutan
- Sri Lanka
- Maldives

These nations have distinct identities and were never one unified civilisation. Yet their histories intersect through trade, migration, religion, kingdoms and shared geographical networks, creating a regional world that predates modern borders.

Akhand Bharat is a historical-political idea. The Indian Continent is a proposed cultural-geographical framework, not a call to merge nations or claim their territories.

The question is not whether these countries should become one, but whether our inherited continental labels adequately reflect their connected history.
